title: Stars that never set, stars that never rise
subtitle: How your latitude sorts the sky into three zones

sections.heading: Three kinds of star
body: After this lesson you will be able to say, for any star, whether it is always up from Brooklyn, sometimes up, or never up, using nothing but its distance from the pole.

The sky turns around the north celestial pole, and from Brooklyn that pole stands 40.7° above the northern horizon, the same number as your latitude. Picture a circle around the pole that just touches the horizon due north. Its radius is 40.7°. Any star inside that circle turns around the pole without ever reaching the horizon. Such stars are called circumpolar: they are up all night, every night of the year, and in the daytime too, hidden by the bright sky.
There is a matching circle around the south celestial pole, which lies 40.7° below your southern horizon. Stars inside it never climb above the horizon at all. Everything in between rises and sets.

steps.caption: Facing north on an October evening. The circle is 40.7° around the pole and just touches the horizon. The Little Dipper, Cassiopeia, Cepheus and Draco are inside it. The Big Dipper is at its lowest, skimming the rooftops.
Half an hour per second. Watch the end of the Dipper's handle: Alkaid slides along the horizon around midnight and comes back up without quite setting. It sits right on the edge of the circle.
Capella, low in the northeast, is 44° from the pole: just outside the circle. It does set, but for less than four hours out of every 24. Stars farther from the pole spend longer below the horizon.

Facing south in February with the ground switched off, so you can see below the horizon. This circle is the zone that never rises from Brooklyn. Canopus, the second-brightest star in the sky, passes 3° under your horizon, straight below Sirius.

sections.heading: What is circumpolar from Brooklyn
body: A star's distance from the pole is fixed, so you can sort stars by declination, the sky's version of latitude, measured in degrees north or south of the celestial equator. From latitude 40.7° north, stars with a declination above +49.3° (that is, 90 minus 40.7) never set. Stars below −49.3° never rise.

The never-set group includes the Little Dipper ([[con:UMi|Ursa Minor]]), the W of [[con:Cas|Cassiopeia]], [[con:Cep|Cepheus]], [[con:Cam|Camelopardalis]] and nearly all of [[con:Dra|Draco]]. The Big Dipper only just qualifies. Its bowl is safely inside, but [[star:Alkaid|Alkaid]], the star at the tip of the handle, grazes the horizon at its lowest. In practice, when the Dipper is at the bottom of its circle on autumn evenings, city buildings and haze hide it.
The never-rise group includes the Southern Cross, the bright stars Alpha and Beta Centauri, [[star:Canopus|Canopus]] and the Magellanic Clouds. To see those you have to travel south.

sections.heading: The in-between stars are the seasonal ones
body: Most of the sky lies between the two circles. These stars rise and set, and the farther south a star is, the lower and shorter its arc. [[star:Vega|Vega]], well to the north, is above the horizon for about 18 hours out of 24. [[star:Antares|Antares]], far to the south, manages only about 9, and never gets higher than two and a half fists.

Because these stars spend part of each day below the horizon, whether you can see one depends on whether its time above the horizon falls at night. That changes through the year, which is why Orion is a winter constellation and Scorpius a summer one. The circumpolar stars have no season. They only change position: the Dipper is high on spring evenings and low on autumn ones.

steps.caption: Drag the latitude slider and watch Polaris. Go north and the pole climbs, so the never-set circle grows; at the North Pole it covers the whole visible sky. Go south to the equator and the pole drops to the horizon: nothing is circumpolar and every star rises and sets.

sections.tryIt: Find Cassiopeia's W tonight, then find it again at the same time in three months. It will be in a different part of its circle around Polaris, but it will be there. Try the same with Orion and one of those two nights it will be missing.

keyPoints: The pole's height above the horizon equals your latitude: 40.7° in Brooklyn.
Stars within 40.7° of the north celestial pole never set from Brooklyn; stars within 40.7° of the south celestial pole never rise.
Circumpolar from Brooklyn: the Little Dipper, Cassiopeia, Cepheus, Draco, Camelopardalis, and (barely) the Big Dipper.
Everything in between rises and sets, and is seen at night only in its season.

questions.prompt: From latitude 40.7° north, which stars never set?
choices: Those within 40.7° of the north celestial pole
Those within 49.3° of the north celestial pole
Those within 40.7° of the celestial equator
Only Polaris
questions.explanation: The circumpolar circle has a radius equal to your latitude, because the pole stands that many degrees above the northern horizon.

questions.prompt: Why can you never see the Southern Cross from Brooklyn?
choices: It is too faint for city skies
It is only up during the daytime
It is hidden behind the Milky Way
It lies within 40.7° of the south celestial pole, so it never rises
questions.explanation: Stars closer than your latitude to the opposite pole stay below the horizon all day and all year. The Cross is about 30° from the south celestial pole.

questions.prompt: You move from Brooklyn to Anchorage, Alaska (latitude 61° north). What happens to the circumpolar region?
choices: It shrinks, because the pole is lower
It grows, because the pole is higher
It stays the same size but moves south
It disappears
questions.explanation: The never-set circle has a radius equal to your latitude. At 61° north many more stars, including Vega and Capella, never set.

questions.prompt: Cassiopeia is circumpolar from Brooklyn. What does that tell you about seeing it in July?
choices: It is below the horizon in July
It is visible only before dawn
It is up all night; only its position around Polaris differs
It can be seen only from a dark site
questions.explanation: Circumpolar constellations are above the horizon at every hour of every night. The season changes where they sit around the pole, not whether they are up.

questions.prompt: From the equator (latitude 0°), how much of the sky is circumpolar?
choices: All of it
The northern half
A circle 23.4° across
None of it
questions.explanation: At the equator both poles lie on the horizon, so the never-set circle has zero radius: every star rises and sets.
